standard.title: Compare text types
standard.description: describe some similarities and differences between imaginative, informative and persuasive texts
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can identify some differences between imaginative and informative texts (AC9EFLY03). They have not yet described similarities and differences systematically across all three text type categories — imaginative, informative and persuasive.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students describe similarities and differences between imaginative, informative and persuasive texts.

nodes.label: Three text type categories
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can name imaginative, informative and persuasive as three categories of text and give an example of each.
nodes.minimum_width: Name the three text type categories and give one example of each.
nodes.typical_width: Name and describe the three text type categories, give multiple examples of each, and explain what each category is trying to do.
wider: Collect examples of each text type category from classroom and home environments
Discuss how digital texts fit into these categories — does a website belong to one or more categories?
success_criteria: Student correctly names all three text type categories
Student gives a plausible example of each

nodes.label: Describing differences between text types
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can describe differences between imaginative, informative and persuasive texts — in purpose, features, and language.
nodes.minimum_width: Describe at least two differences between two of the three text types.
nodes.typical_width: Describe differences in purpose, structural features and language between imaginative, informative and persuasive texts, using specific text examples as evidence.
wider: Compare texts that 'tell stories' with those that 'give opinions' — discuss what features distinguish them
Find examples where a text has features of more than one type and discuss which category fits best
nodes.hinge_reason: Students who do not have a working three-category schema — particularly if persuasive remains conflated with informative — cannot select appropriate text types for a given purpose in N3, which is the descriptor's application endpoint.

response_modes.reason: Students often know that stories and information books are different but struggle to articulate persuasive as a distinct category. Encountering opinion texts — simple reviews, letters of request — as a third category alongside examples clarifies the distinction.

success_criteria: Student describes at least two differences between two text types with feature-based reasoning
Student correctly categorises a new example text when presented

nodes.label: Selecting texts for a purpose
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can select a text type appropriate for a given purpose or task and explain their choice.
nodes.minimum_width: Given a specific task (e.g. find out how something works; enjoy a story; decide which is better), identify which text type would be most useful and explain why.
nodes.typical_width: Select appropriate texts for a range of tasks — finding information, entertainment, forming an opinion — and justify the selection by linking text type to purpose.
wider: Explore how the same topic might be addressed by all three text types (e.g. an animal could be in a story, a report, or an advertisement) and discuss what each offers
Evaluate a text choice — did it serve the purpose well? What would a different text type offer?

response_modes.reason: Selecting a text for a purpose requires students to integrate understanding of all three text types — it is the practical application that makes the category distinctions useful and demonstrates genuine understanding.

success_criteria: Student selects an appropriate text type for a given task
Student explains their choice by linking the text type to the task's purpose
